NUS ST5207 — Nonparametric Regression¶

Theory, Algorithms, Experiments, and a Real-Data Case Study¶

This notebook is a tutorial-style companion to the main ideas typically associated with nonparametric regression:

  1. Parametric vs nonparametric modelling
  2. Histograms and density estimation
  3. Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)
  4. Kernel regression / Nadaraya–Watson estimator
  5. Local polynomial regression
  6. Bandwidth and smoothing-parameter selection
  7. Regression splines
  8. Smoothing splines
  9. Additive models / GAM-like models
  10. Semiparametric regression
  11. Bias–variance trade-off
  12. Curse of dimensionality
  13. Consistency and convergence-rate intuition
  14. Real-data case study

The notebook deliberately combines:

  • mathematical intuition,
  • from-scratch implementations,
  • established Python libraries,
  • visualization,
  • hyperparameter experimentation,
  • cross-validation,
  • model comparison.

Case study dataset: Auto MPG data, downloaded directly from the UCI Machine Learning Repository when this notebook runs.

The core prediction problem is:

[ Y = m(X) + \varepsilon ]

where the unknown regression function (m(\cdot)) is estimated without forcing it to have a fixed global form such as a straight line.

Environment ready.

1. Parametric vs Nonparametric Regression¶

A parametric model assumes that the relationship belongs to a predefined finite-dimensional family.

For example:

[ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon ]

or

[ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2 + \varepsilon. ]

The unknown object is a finite parameter vector:

[ \theta = (\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots). ]

A nonparametric model instead estimates an unknown function:

[ Y = m(X)+\varepsilon. ]

The function (m(x)) may be nonlinear and its effective complexity can increase with the amount of data.

Examples include:

  • kernel regression,
  • local polynomial regression,
  • smoothing splines,
  • regression splines,
  • additive models.

The flexibility is useful, but it creates an important trade-off:

[ \text{More flexibility} \Rightarrow \text{lower bias but potentially higher variance}. ]

In [2]:
# Synthetic nonlinear regression problem

n = 300
X = np.sort(np.random.uniform(0, 10, size=n))
true_f = 2 + np.sin(X) + 0.15 * X
y = true_f + np.random.normal(0, 0.35, size=n)

X2 = X.reshape(-1, 1)

linear = LinearRegression().fit(X2, y)
pred_linear = linear.predict(X2)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=18, alpha=0.5, label="observations")
plt.plot(X, true_f, linewidth=3, label="true regression function")
plt.plot(X, pred_linear, linewidth=2, label="linear regression")
plt.xlabel("X")
plt.ylabel("Y")
plt.title("Parametric linear regression underfits a nonlinear relationship")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

2. Histograms as Nonparametric Density Estimators¶

Before regression, it is useful to understand the simpler problem of density estimation.

Given observations

[ X_1,\ldots,X_n, ]

we wish to estimate their unknown density (f(x)).

A histogram partitions the domain into bins of width (h). For a bin (B_j),

[ \hat f(x)¶

\frac{#{X_i\in B_j}}{nh}, \qquad x\in B_j. ]

The bin width acts as a smoothing parameter.

  • too small (h): highly variable estimate,
  • too large (h): excessive smoothing.

This same bias–variance principle reappears in KDE and regression smoothing.

In [3]:
sample = np.concatenate([
    np.random.normal(-1.2, 0.6, 400),
    np.random.normal(1.5, 0.9, 600),
])

for bins in [8, 20, 60]:
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.hist(sample, bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.7)
    plt.title(f"Histogram density estimate: bins={bins}")
    plt.xlabel("x")
    plt.ylabel("estimated density")
    plt.show()

3. Kernel Density Estimation¶

A histogram estimate is discontinuous and strongly dependent on arbitrary bin boundaries.

Kernel Density Estimation replaces bins with smooth local contributions:

[ \hat f_h(x)¶

\frac{1}{nh} \sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right). ]

Here:

  • (K) is the kernel,
  • (h>0) is the bandwidth.

A Gaussian kernel is

[ K(u)¶

\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-u^2/2}. ]

The bandwidth usually matters much more than the exact kernel choice.

In [4]:
def gaussian_kernel(u):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * u**2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)

def kde_1d(x_eval, x_train, bandwidth):
    x_eval = np.asarray(x_eval)[:, None]
    x_train = np.asarray(x_train)[None, :]
    u = (x_eval - x_train) / bandwidth
    return gaussian_kernel(u).mean(axis=1) / bandwidth

grid = np.linspace(sample.min() - 1, sample.max() + 1, 500)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.hist(sample, bins=25, density=True, alpha=0.25, label="histogram")

for h in [0.12, 0.35, 0.9]:
    plt.plot(grid, kde_1d(grid, sample, h), linewidth=2, label=f"KDE h={h}")

plt.title("Kernel Density Estimation and bandwidth sensitivity")
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("density")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

3.1 KDE Bias–Variance Intuition¶

For many smooth densities, the leading terms behave approximately like

[ \mathrm{Bias}[\hat f_h(x)] = O(h^2), ]

and

[ \mathrm{Var}[\hat f_h(x)]¶

O\left(\frac{1}{nh}\right). ]

Therefore,

[ \mathrm{MSE} \approx C_1 h^4 + \frac{C_2}{nh}. ]

Balancing the two terms yields the famous one-dimensional order

[ h_{\mathrm{opt}}¶

O(n^{-1/5}). ]

This is one of the central rate calculations in nonparametric statistics.

In [5]:
n_values = np.array([100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000])
rate = n_values ** (-1/5)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(n_values, rate, marker="o")
plt.xscale("log")
plt.yscale("log")
plt.xlabel("sample size n")
plt.ylabel(r"$n^{-1/5}$")
plt.title("Canonical 1D nonparametric bandwidth rate")
plt.show()

4. Kernel Regression — Nadaraya–Watson Estimator¶

For regression,

[ Y_i = m(X_i)+\varepsilon_i, ]

the Nadaraya–Watson estimator is

[ \hat m_h(x)¶

\frac{ \sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right)Y_i }{ \sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right) }. ]

Interpretation:

  1. calculate the distance from (x) to every training observation,
  2. convert distances into kernel weights,
  3. compute a locally weighted average of responses.

The bandwidth (h) controls locality.

In [6]:
class NadarayaWatsonRegressor(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):
    def __init__(self, bandwidth=1.0):
        self.bandwidth = bandwidth

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.X_ = np.asarray(X).reshape(-1)
        self.y_ = np.asarray(y)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X).reshape(-1)
        preds = []

        for x in X:
            u = (x - self.X_) / self.bandwidth
            w = gaussian_kernel(u)

            if w.sum() < 1e-12:
                preds.append(self.y_.mean())
            else:
                preds.append(np.dot(w, self.y_) / w.sum())

        return np.asarray(preds)
In [7]:
grid_reg = np.linspace(X.min(), X.max(), 400)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=15, alpha=0.35)

for h in [0.15, 0.5, 1.5]:
    model = NadarayaWatsonRegressor(bandwidth=h).fit(X, y)
    pred = model.predict(grid_reg)
    plt.plot(grid_reg, pred, linewidth=2, label=f"h={h}")

plt.plot(X, true_f, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="true function")
plt.title("Nadaraya–Watson regression")
plt.xlabel("X")
plt.ylabel("Y")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Interpretation¶

Typical pattern:

  • (h=0.15): follows small fluctuations and noise,
  • (h=0.5): captures the dominant nonlinear structure,
  • (h=1.5): smooth but potentially biased.

This is nonparametric model complexity control.

Unlike a polynomial degree, complexity is not described by a fixed number of coefficients. Instead it is primarily controlled through the smoothing parameter.

5. Local Polynomial Regression¶

The Nadaraya–Watson estimator is also called a local constant estimator.

Near a query point (x_0), it effectively assumes:

[ m(x)\approx \beta_0. ]

Local linear regression instead approximates

[ m(x) \approx \beta_0+\beta_1(x-x_0). ]

For each query point (x_0), solve

[ \min_{\beta_0,\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^n K\left( \frac{X_i-x_0}{h} \right) \left[ Y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1(X_i-x_0) \right]^2. ]

Then

[ \hat m(x_0)=\hat\beta_0. ]

A major advantage is reduced boundary bias.

In [8]:
def local_polynomial_predict(x_train, y_train, x_eval, bandwidth, degree=1):
    x_train = np.asarray(x_train)
    y_train = np.asarray(y_train)
    x_eval = np.asarray(x_eval)

    preds = []

    for x0 in x_eval:
        dx = x_train - x0
        w = gaussian_kernel(dx / bandwidth)

        # Design matrix:
        # [1, dx, dx^2, ..., dx^degree]
        A = np.column_stack([dx ** j for j in range(degree + 1)])

        W = np.sqrt(w)[:, None]
        Aw = A * W
        yw = y_train * W[:, 0]

        beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Aw, yw, rcond=None)
        preds.append(beta[0])

    return np.asarray(preds)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=15, alpha=0.3)

for degree in [0, 1, 2]:
    pred = local_polynomial_predict(
        X, y, grid_reg,
        bandwidth=0.5,
        degree=degree
    )
    plt.plot(grid_reg, pred, linewidth=2, label=f"degree={degree}")

plt.plot(X, true_f, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="true function")
plt.title("Local constant vs local linear vs local quadratic smoothing")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

6. Bandwidth Selection by Cross-Validation¶

The bandwidth should normally be selected from the data.

A common objective is leave-one-out cross-validation:

[ CV(h)¶

\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ Y_i-\hat m_{-i,h}(X_i) \right]^2. ]

Here (\hat m_{-i,h}) is fitted without observation (i).

The bandwidth minimizing this estimate is selected.

In [9]:
def loo_cv_nw(x, y, bandwidth):
    x = np.asarray(x)
    y = np.asarray(y)
    errors = []

    for i in range(len(x)):
        mask = np.arange(len(x)) != i

        model = NadarayaWatsonRegressor(
            bandwidth=bandwidth
        ).fit(x[mask], y[mask])

        pred = model.predict([x[i]])[0]
        errors.append((y[i] - pred) ** 2)

    return np.mean(errors)

candidate_h = np.linspace(0.1, 1.5, 20)
cv_scores = [loo_cv_nw(X, y, h) for h in candidate_h]

best_h = candidate_h[np.argmin(cv_scores)]
print("Best bandwidth:", best_h)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(candidate_h, cv_scores, marker="o")
plt.axvline(best_h, linestyle="--")
plt.xlabel("bandwidth")
plt.ylabel("LOOCV MSE")
plt.title("Bandwidth selection using leave-one-out CV")
plt.show()

Best bandwidth: 0.24736842105263157
In [10]:
best_nw = NadarayaWatsonRegressor(best_h).fit(X, y)
best_pred = best_nw.predict(grid_reg)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=15, alpha=0.3)
plt.plot(grid_reg, best_pred, linewidth=3, label=f"CV-selected h={best_h:.3f}")
plt.plot(X, true_f, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="true function")
plt.title("Cross-validation selected kernel regression")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

7. Boundary Bias¶

Kernel regression behaves differently near the boundaries of the predictor domain.

At an interior point, observations are usually available on both sides.

Near an edge, kernel support becomes asymmetric, which can distort a local constant estimate.

Local linear regression partially corrects this by fitting a local slope.

In [11]:
# Boundary-focused synthetic dataset
xb = np.linspace(0, 3, 120)
yb_true = np.exp(-0.7 * xb) + 0.2 * xb
yb = yb_true + np.random.normal(0, 0.05, len(xb))

grid_b = np.linspace(0, 3, 300)

nw_b = NadarayaWatsonRegressor(0.45).fit(xb, yb).predict(grid_b)
ll_b = local_polynomial_predict(xb, yb, grid_b, bandwidth=0.45, degree=1)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(xb, yb, s=15, alpha=0.35)
plt.plot(grid_b, np.exp(-0.7 * grid_b) + 0.2 * grid_b, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="true")
plt.plot(grid_b, nw_b, linewidth=2, label="local constant")
plt.plot(grid_b, ll_b, linewidth=2, label="local linear")
plt.title("Boundary behaviour of local smoothers")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

8. Regression Splines¶

Splines approximate an unknown smooth function using piecewise polynomials joined at points called knots.

A spline model can be represented as

[ m(x)¶

\sum_{j=1}^{K} \beta_j B_j(x), ]

where (B_j(x)) are basis functions.

Compared with fitting one high-degree global polynomial, splines are:

  • more numerically stable,
  • more local,
  • much less prone to extreme oscillation.

Common spline families include:

  • truncated power bases,
  • B-splines,
  • natural cubic splines.
In [12]:
spline_model = Pipeline([
    ("spline", SplineTransformer(
        degree=3,
        n_knots=8,
        include_bias=False
    )),
    ("regressor", LinearRegression())
])

spline_model.fit(X2, y)
pred_spline = spline_model.predict(grid_reg.reshape(-1, 1))

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=15, alpha=0.3)
plt.plot(grid_reg, pred_spline, linewidth=3, label="cubic regression spline")
plt.plot(X, true_f, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="true function")
plt.title("Regression spline")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

8.1 Knot Count as a Complexity Parameter¶

More knots create a richer basis.

This resembles bandwidth selection:

  • many knots → low bias / high variance,
  • few knots → high bias / low variance.
In [13]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=12, alpha=0.25)

for n_knots in [4, 7, 15, 30]:
    model = Pipeline([
        ("spline", SplineTransformer(
            degree=3,
            n_knots=n_knots,
            include_bias=False
        )),
        ("regressor", LinearRegression())
    ])

    model.fit(X2, y)
    pred = model.predict(grid_reg.reshape(-1, 1))
    plt.plot(grid_reg, pred, linewidth=2, label=f"{n_knots} knots")

plt.title("Regression spline flexibility")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

9. Penalized / Smoothing-Spline Idea¶

Regression splines control complexity partly through the number and position of knots.

Smoothing splines instead optimize a penalized criterion:

[ \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-f(X_i))^2 + \lambda \int [f''(x)]^2dx. ]

The first term rewards fit.

The second penalizes curvature.

Hence:

  • small (\lambda): flexible / wiggly,
  • large (\lambda): smooth,
  • (\lambda\to\infty): approaches a straight line.

scipy.interpolate.UnivariateSpline uses a related smoothing formulation controlled by s.

In [14]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=15, alpha=0.25)

for s in [5, 20, 80]:
    us = UnivariateSpline(X, y, s=s)
    plt.plot(grid_reg, us(grid_reg), linewidth=2, label=f"s={s}")

plt.plot(X, true_f, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="true function")
plt.title("Smoothing spline behaviour")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

10. Penalized Spline Basis with Ridge Regression¶

Another practical construction is:

  1. create many spline basis functions,
  2. penalize coefficients with Ridge regression.

[ \hat\beta¶

\arg\min_\beta \left{ |y-B\beta|_2^2 + \alpha |\beta|_2^2 \right}. ]

This connects nonparametric smoothing to regularization.

In [15]:
penalized_spline = Pipeline([
    ("spline", SplineTransformer(
        degree=3,
        n_knots=20,
        include_bias=False
    )),
    ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=1.0))
])

param_grid = {
    "ridge__alpha": np.logspace(-4, 3, 20)
}

grid_search = GridSearchCV(
    penalized_spline,
    param_grid,
    cv=5,
    scoring="neg_mean_squared_error",
    n_jobs=-1
)

grid_search.fit(X2, y)

print("Best alpha:", grid_search.best_params_["ridge__alpha"])

pred_pen = grid_search.predict(grid_reg.reshape(-1, 1))

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=15, alpha=0.25)
plt.plot(grid_reg, pred_pen, linewidth=3, label="CV penalized spline")
plt.plot(X, true_f, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="true")
plt.title("Penalized spline regression")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Best alpha: 0.08858667904100823

11. Additive Models¶

For several predictors, fully multivariate nonparametric smoothing quickly becomes difficult.

An additive model assumes

[ Y¶

\beta_0 + f_1(X_1) + f_2(X_2) + \cdots + f_p(X_p) + \varepsilon. ]

Each individual effect can remain nonlinear, while the decomposition avoids estimating an unrestricted (p)-dimensional surface.

This is the basic structure behind Generalized Additive Models (GAMs).

In [16]:
# Synthetic additive data

n = 800

x1 = np.random.uniform(-3, 3, n)
x2 = np.random.uniform(0, 5, n)

y_add = (
    np.sin(x1)
    + 0.35 * (x2 - 2.5) ** 2
    + np.random.normal(0, 0.3, n)
)

X_add = np.column_stack([x1, x2])

# Build spline bases separately, concatenate, then regress.
s1 = SplineTransformer(n_knots=8, degree=3, include_bias=False)
s2 = SplineTransformer(n_knots=8, degree=3, include_bias=False)

B1 = s1.fit_transform(x1.reshape(-1, 1))
B2 = s2.fit_transform(x2.reshape(-1, 1))

B = np.column_stack([B1, B2])

add_model = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(B, y_add)
pred_add = add_model.predict(B)

print("Training R2:", r2_score(y_add, pred_add))
print("Training RMSE:", mean_squared_error(y_add, pred_add) ** 0.5)

Training R2: 0.9083295378829317
Training RMSE: 0.3108576881816311

Recovering Partial Effects¶

To visualize (f_1(x_1)), vary (x_1) while holding the (x_2)-basis contribution at a reference value.

Similarly for (f_2(x_2)).

In [17]:
grid1 = np.linspace(x1.min(), x1.max(), 300)
grid2 = np.linspace(x2.min(), x2.max(), 300)

coef1 = add_model.coef_[:B1.shape[1]]
coef2 = add_model.coef_[B1.shape[1]:]

effect1 = s1.transform(grid1.reshape(-1,1)) @ coef1
effect2 = s2.transform(grid2.reshape(-1,1)) @ coef2

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(grid1, effect1, linewidth=3)
plt.xlabel("x1")
plt.ylabel("estimated partial effect")
plt.title("Estimated additive effect f1(x1)")
plt.show()

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(grid2, effect2, linewidth=3)
plt.xlabel("x2")
plt.ylabel("estimated partial effect")
plt.title("Estimated additive effect f2(x2)")
plt.show()

12. Semiparametric Regression¶

A semiparametric model mixes parametric and nonparametric components.

A canonical example is the partially linear model:

[ Y¶

Z^\top\beta + g(X) + \varepsilon. ]

Here:

  • (Z^\top\beta) is parametric,
  • (g(X)) is nonparametric.

This is useful when:

  • some effects are believed to be approximately linear,
  • another predictor requires flexible nonlinear modelling,
  • interpretable coefficients are still desirable.
In [18]:
# Synthetic partially linear example

n = 700

x = np.random.uniform(0, 8, n)
z = np.random.normal(size=n)

g_true = 1.5 * np.sin(x / 1.3)
beta_true = 2.2

y_semi = beta_true * z + g_true + np.random.normal(0, 0.4, n)

# Nonparametric part approximated with spline basis.
spline = SplineTransformer(n_knots=10, degree=3, include_bias=False)
Bx = spline.fit_transform(x.reshape(-1, 1))

design = np.column_stack([z, Bx])

semi_model = Ridge(alpha=0.1).fit(design, y_semi)

beta_hat = semi_model.coef_[0]

print("True linear coefficient:", beta_true)
print("Estimated linear coefficient:", beta_hat)

True linear coefficient: 2.2
Estimated linear coefficient: 2.175560968342789
In [19]:
grid_x = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 300)

coef_g = semi_model.coef_[1:]
g_hat = spline.transform(grid_x.reshape(-1,1)) @ coef_g

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 4))
plt.plot(grid_x, 1.5*np.sin(grid_x/1.3), linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="true g(x)")
plt.plot(grid_x, g_hat, linewidth=3, label="estimated g(x)")
plt.title("Nonparametric component of a partially linear model")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

13. Curse of Dimensionality¶

Nonparametric methods rely on local observations.

In one dimension, a small neighbourhood may still contain many samples.

In higher dimensions, volume grows rapidly.

For a (d)-dimensional hypercube with side width (r),

[ V=r^d. ]

If (r=0.1):

  • (d=1): (10^{-1}),
  • (d=2): (10^{-2}),
  • (d=5): (10^{-5}),
  • (d=10): (10^{-10}).

Thus huge datasets may be required to populate local neighbourhoods.

This motivates:

  • additive assumptions,
  • dimensionality reduction,
  • structural constraints,
  • regularization,
  • semiparametric models.
In [20]:
dims = np.arange(1, 11)
r = 0.1
volumes = r ** dims

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(dims, volumes, marker="o")
plt.yscale("log")
plt.xlabel("dimension d")
plt.ylabel(r"volume $0.1^d$")
plt.title("Exponential shrinkage of local neighbourhood volume")
plt.show()

14. Real-Data Case Study — Auto MPG¶

We now apply the ideas to a real dataset.

The Auto MPG dataset contains fuel-efficiency and vehicle-engine characteristics.

We will download it directly from the UCI Machine Learning Repository.

Main response variable:

[ Y=\text{mpg} ]

Key predictor for nonparametric analysis:

[ X=\text{horsepower}. ]

We will investigate whether fuel efficiency has a nonlinear relationship with horsepower.

Later we will create a partially additive model using several predictors.

In [21]:
# Download the real dataset directly from UCI.

14.1 First Baseline — Linear Regression¶

A global linear model assumes

[ E[\text{mpg}\mid\text{horsepower}]¶

\beta_0+\beta_1\text{horsepower}. ]

We will compare this with more flexible alternatives.

In [24]:
X_hp = auto[["horsepower"]].to_numpy()
y_mpg = auto["mpg"].to_numpy()

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_hp,
    y_mpg,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=42
)

linear_hp = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_linear = linear_hp.predict(X_test)

def metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    return {
        "RMSE": mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred) ** 0.5,
        "MAE": mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred),
        "R2": r2_score(y_true, y_pred),
    }

metrics(y_test, pred_linear)
Out[24]:
{'RMSE': 4.680724435839859, 'MAE': 3.781267671503429, 'R2': 0.5655794324593799}

14.2 Kernel Regression with Cross-Validated Bandwidth¶

In [25]:
# Manual CV over the training set.
# Use a modest grid because the estimator is O(n_train * n_eval).

hp_train_1d = X_train.ravel()

bandwidths = np.linspace(5, 60, 25)

kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

cv_rmse = []

for h in bandwidths:
    fold_rmse = []

    for tr_idx, va_idx in kf.split(hp_train_1d):
        model = NadarayaWatsonRegressor(h).fit(
            hp_train_1d[tr_idx],
            y_train[tr_idx]
        )

        pred = model.predict(hp_train_1d[va_idx])
        fold_rmse.append(
            mean_squared_error(y_train[va_idx], pred) ** 0.5
        )

    cv_rmse.append(np.mean(fold_rmse))

best_h_real = bandwidths[np.argmin(cv_rmse)]

print("Best real-data bandwidth:", best_h_real)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(bandwidths, cv_rmse, marker="o")
plt.axvline(best_h_real, linestyle="--")
plt.xlabel("bandwidth")
plt.ylabel("CV RMSE")
plt.title("Bandwidth selection on Auto MPG")
plt.show()

Best real-data bandwidth: 5.0
In [26]:
nw_real = NadarayaWatsonRegressor(best_h_real).fit(
    hp_train_1d,
    y_train
)

pred_nw = nw_real.predict(X_test.ravel())

metrics(y_test, pred_nw)

14.3 Regression Spline¶

We tune the number of knots by cross-validation.

In [27]:
spline_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("spline", SplineTransformer(
        degree=3,
        include_bias=False
    )),
    ("ridge", Ridge())
])

param_grid = {
    "spline__n_knots": [4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12],
    "ridge__alpha": [0.0, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0]
}

search = GridSearchCV(
    spline_pipe,
    param_grid,
    scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
    cv=5,
    n_jobs=-1
)

search.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("Best params:", search.best_params_)
print("Best CV RMSE:", -search.best_score_)

pred_spline_real = search.predict(X_test)

metrics(y_test, pred_spline_real)

Best params: {'ridge__alpha': 0.1, 'spline__n_knots': 8}

14.4 Gaussian Kernel Ridge Regression¶

Kernel ridge regression is not identical to Nadaraya–Watson smoothing, but it provides an important connection between:

  • kernels,
  • regularization,
  • flexible nonlinear regression.

It solves a penalized objective in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space.

In [28]:
kr = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", KernelRidge(kernel="rbf"))
])

kr_grid = {
    "model__alpha": [0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0],
    "model__gamma": [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0]
}

kr_search = GridSearchCV(
    kr,
    kr_grid,
    cv=5,
    scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
    n_jobs=-1
)

kr_search.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("Best params:", kr_search.best_params_)

pred_kr = kr_search.predict(X_test)

metrics(y_test, pred_kr)

Best params: {'model__alpha': 0.1, 'model__gamma': 0.5}
Out[28]:
{'RMSE': 4.038986044806033, 'MAE': 3.165415637776419, 'R2': 0.6765337782264624}

15. Multivariable Additive Case Study¶

A one-dimensional smoother is useful for interpretation, but fuel efficiency depends on several variables.

We now estimate a model of the form

[ \text{mpg}¶

\beta_0 + f_1(\text{horsepower}) + f_2(\text{weight}) + f_3(\text{acceleration}) + f_4(\text{model year}) + \varepsilon. ]

Each (f_j) is represented with a spline basis.

This is a practical GAM-like additive model.

In [31]:
features = [
    "horsepower",
    "weight",
    "acceleration",
    "model_year",
]

X_multi = auto[features].copy()
y_multi = auto["mpg"].to_numpy()

X_train_m, X_test_m, y_train_m, y_test_m = train_test_split(
    X_multi,
    y_multi,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=42
)

# Build one spline transformer per feature manually.
transformers = {}

def fit_additive_basis(df, n_knots=7):
    blocks = []

    for col in df.columns:
        tr = SplineTransformer(
            n_knots=n_knots,
            degree=3,
            include_bias=False
        )

        B = tr.fit_transform(df[[col]])
        transformers[col] = tr
        blocks.append(B)

    return np.column_stack(blocks)

B_train = fit_additive_basis(X_train_m)

def transform_additive_basis(df):
    blocks = []

    for col in df.columns:
        blocks.append(
            transformers[col].transform(df[[col]])
        )

    return np.column_stack(blocks)

B_test = transform_additive_basis(X_test_m)

additive_ridge = Ridge(alpha=1.0)
additive_ridge.fit(B_train, y_train_m)

pred_add_test = additive_ridge.predict(B_test)

metrics(y_test_m, pred_add_test)
Out[31]:
{'RMSE': 2.4510430343248206,
 'MAE': 1.7551411101596635,
 'R2': 0.8808796108608193}

15.1 Tune the Additive Model Regularization¶

In [32]:
alphas = np.logspace(-3, 3, 20)

best_alpha = None
best_score = np.inf

kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

for alpha in alphas:
    fold_scores = []

    for tr_idx, va_idx in kf.split(B_train):
        model = Ridge(alpha=alpha)
        model.fit(B_train[tr_idx], y_train_m[tr_idx])

        pred = model.predict(B_train[va_idx])

        fold_scores.append(
            mean_squared_error(
                y_train_m[va_idx],
                pred
            ) ** 0.5
        )

    score = np.mean(fold_scores)

    if score < best_score:
        best_score = score
        best_alpha = alpha

print("Best alpha:", best_alpha)
print("CV RMSE:", best_score)

additive_ridge = Ridge(alpha=best_alpha).fit(
    B_train,
    y_train_m
)

pred_add_test = additive_ridge.predict(B_test)

metrics(y_test_m, pred_add_test)

Best alpha: 0.6951927961775606
CV RMSE: 2.9877575998829977

16. Partial Effects from the Additive Model¶

Because the model is additive, we can inspect the estimated contribution of each variable separately.

The curves are centered for easier interpretation.

In [33]:
offset = 0

for col in features:
    tr = transformers[col]
    n_basis = tr.n_features_out_

    coef = additive_ridge.coef_[offset:offset+n_basis]

    grid = np.linspace(
        X_train_m[col].min(),
        X_train_m[col].max(),
        250
    )

    Bgrid = tr.transform(
        pd.DataFrame({col: grid})
    )

    effect = Bgrid @ coef
    effect = effect - effect.mean()

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.plot(grid, effect, linewidth=3)
    plt.xlabel(col)
    plt.ylabel("centered partial effect")
    plt.title(f"Estimated additive effect: {col}")
    plt.show()

    offset += n_basis

17. Semiparametric Auto MPG Model¶

Suppose we believe:

  • horsepower has a nonlinear effect,
  • model year has an approximately linear trend.

Then we can fit

[ \text{mpg}¶

\beta_0 + \beta_1\text{model year} + g(\text{horsepower}) + \varepsilon. ]

This gives the interpretability of a linear coefficient while preserving nonlinear flexibility for horsepower.

In [34]:
semi_df = auto[["horsepower", "model_year", "mpg"]].copy()

X_train_s, X_test_s, y_train_s, y_test_s = train_test_split(
    semi_df[["horsepower", "model_year"]],
    semi_df["mpg"],
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=42
)

hp_spline = SplineTransformer(
    n_knots=8,
    degree=3,
    include_bias=False
)

Bhp_train = hp_spline.fit_transform(
    X_train_s[["horsepower"]]
)

Bhp_test = hp_spline.transform(
    X_test_s[["horsepower"]]
)

Z_train = np.column_stack([
    X_train_s["model_year"].to_numpy(),
    Bhp_train
])

Z_test = np.column_stack([
    X_test_s["model_year"].to_numpy(),
    Bhp_test
])

semi_real = Ridge(alpha=0.1).fit(Z_train, y_train_s)

pred_semi_real = semi_real.predict(Z_test)

print("Estimated model-year linear coefficient:",
      semi_real.coef_[0])

metrics(y_test_s, pred_semi_real)

Estimated model-year linear coefficient: 0.6915438859666284
Out[34]:
{'RMSE': 3.3903303244521332,
 'MAE': 2.672286742872789,
 'R2': 0.7720874402300539}

18. Bias–Variance Simulation¶

We now make the bias–variance trade-off visible empirically.

For a fixed evaluation point (x_0), repeatedly generate noisy datasets and estimate

[ \hat m_h(x_0). ]

Then estimate:

[ \operatorname{Bias}^2¶

(E[\hat m_h(x_0)]-m(x_0))^2 ]

and

[ \operatorname{Variance}¶

E[ (\hat m_h(x_0)-E[\hat m_h(x_0)])^2 ]. ]

In [35]:
def true_fun(x):
    return np.sin(x) + 0.15*x + 2

def bias_variance_experiment(
    bandwidth,
    n_rep=150,
    n_sample=120,
    x0=5.0
):
    estimates = []

    for _ in range(n_rep):
        xs = np.sort(
            np.random.uniform(0, 10, n_sample)
        )

        ys = true_fun(xs) + np.random.normal(
            0,
            0.4,
            n_sample
        )

        model = NadarayaWatsonRegressor(
            bandwidth
        ).fit(xs, ys)

        estimates.append(
            model.predict([x0])[0]
        )

    estimates = np.asarray(estimates)

    bias2 = (
        estimates.mean() - true_fun(x0)
    ) ** 2

    variance = estimates.var()

    return bias2, variance

hs = np.linspace(0.1, 2.0, 20)

bias2_values = []
var_values = []

for h in hs:
    b, v = bias_variance_experiment(h)
    bias2_values.append(b)
    var_values.append(v)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.plot(hs, bias2_values, marker="o", label="bias²")
plt.plot(hs, var_values, marker="o", label="variance")
plt.plot(
    hs,
    np.array(bias2_values) + np.array(var_values),
    marker="o",
    label="bias² + variance"
)
plt.xlabel("bandwidth")
plt.ylabel("estimated contribution")
plt.title("Bias–variance trade-off for kernel regression")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

19. Computational Complexity¶

The naive Nadaraya–Watson prediction algorithm compares each query point against every training observation.

For:

  • (n) training samples,
  • (m) prediction locations,

the naive complexity is approximately

[ \Theta(mn). ]

Storage is

[ \Theta(n). ]

For very large datasets this can become expensive.

Possible accelerations include:

  • binning,
  • KD-trees / ball trees for compact-support kernels,
  • approximate nearest neighbours,
  • low-rank kernel approximations,
  • random Fourier features,
  • spline bases,
  • subsampling,
  • GPU vectorization.

Regression splines are often much faster at prediction time because, after fitting, evaluation depends mainly on the number of basis functions rather than all training observations.

20. Key Comparisons¶

Method Main Complexity Control Strength Limitation
Histogram bin width simple density estimate discontinuous
KDE bandwidth smooth density bandwidth sensitive
Nadaraya–Watson bandwidth intuitive local smoother boundary bias; expensive
Local linear bandwidth better boundary behaviour repeated weighted LS
Regression spline knots / basis size efficient and stable knot/basis choice
Smoothing spline smoothness penalty elegant regularization tuning required
Additive model basis + penalties handles several predictors assumes additivity
Semiparametric model parametric + smooth components interpretability + flexibility structure must be chosen

A recurring theme is that almost every method solves the same statistical problem in a different way:

[ \boxed{ \text{Choose enough flexibility to capture signal, but not so much that noise is learned.} } ]

21. Exercises¶

Exercise 1 — KDE¶

Replace the Gaussian kernel with:

  • uniform,
  • triangular,
  • Epanechnikov.

Compare the estimates while keeping bandwidth fixed.

Exercise 2 — Kernel Regression¶

Implement Epanechnikov-weighted Nadaraya–Watson regression.

Exercise 3 — Local Polynomial¶

Compare polynomial degrees 0, 1, 2, and 3 using cross-validation.

Exercise 4 — Splines¶

Tune:

  • spline degree,
  • number of knots,
  • Ridge penalty.

Exercise 5 — Auto MPG¶

Repeat the univariate analysis for:

  • weight,
  • displacement,
  • acceleration.

Exercise 6 — Additive Model¶

Add cylinders and origin to the additive model.

Think carefully about whether they should be:

  • smooth numeric effects,
  • categorical effects,
  • parametric linear effects.

Exercise 7 — Curse of Dimensionality¶

Simulate kernel regression in dimensions: [ d=1,2,4,8. ] Measure the sample size required to maintain similar test error.

Exercise 8 — Model Selection¶

Compare:

  • linear regression,
  • spline regression,
  • additive spline model,
  • Random Forest,
  • Gradient Boosting.

Then discuss the distinction between:

  • predictive performance,
  • interpretability,
  • statistical smoothness,
  • extrapolation.

22. Final Concept Map¶

The central ST5207-style progression can be remembered as:

[ \boxed{ \text{Histogram} \rightarrow \text{KDE} \rightarrow \text{Kernel Regression} \rightarrow \text{Local Polynomial} \rightarrow \text{Splines} \rightarrow \text{Additive Models} \rightarrow \text{Semiparametric Models} } ]

Underlying all of them are the same ideas:

[ \boxed{ \text{local information} + \text{smoothness} + \text{regularization} + \text{cross-validation} + \text{bias–variance trade-off} } ]

The important conceptual shift from ordinary regression is:

Instead of choosing a fixed global equation first and estimating only its parameters, we estimate the shape of the regression function itself from the data.
